22234-aunt-jo-s-scrap-bag-volume-5:
Louisa May Alcott issued the fifth volume of Aunt Jo's Scrap-Bag as her scrap-bag series of stories grew. Volume 5 gathers tales for the young from her magazine writing. One opens on a boy sitting despondent on a doorstep. His eyes are fixed on a pair of very shabby shoes, and his elbows hide the big patches on his knees.

Alcott's scrap-bag held stories of poor children, proud children, and children learning kindness. She wrote them fast, for money and for love, between her larger novels. The moral warmth of Little Women runs through these shorter pieces. Readers who know only the March family will find the same Alcott here in miniature.
22777-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
This fifth volume of a History of the United States, dated 1899, carries the national story from the earliest discovery of America down to the politics of the 1890s. The catalog record names no author. Where the fourth volume ended with Appomattox, this one faces Gilded Age money, tariffs, and pensions.

The contents march through the era's headlines: the so-called Billion Dollar Congress, its Dependent Pensions Act, the McKinley Tariff with Blaine reciprocity, and a new international copyright law. Mr. Blaine appears as Secretary of State. Then come darker notes: a Mafia murder and riot in New Orleans. The Itata affair at San Diego follows. So does American sovereignty assumed over Tutuila in Samoa. The volume is a period summary of a booming, quarrelsome republic.
735-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon reached the medieval world in this fifth volume, with notes by H. H. Milman. It opens with the Franks' conquest of Italy and the temporal power of the popes. It follows the rise and coronation of Charlemagne, then the decay of Roman rule in the West and the rise of the Germanic states. A long section turns east to Arabia.

There Gibbon describes Arabia and its peoples, the birth and doctrine of Mahomet, his preaching at Mecca, and his flight to Medina. The volume thus joins West and East in one sweep, from Frankish kings to the prophet of Islam. It shows Gibbon at his most wide-ranging, and it is vital for readers following Rome into the Middle Ages.
894-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Volume five of Gibbon's history moves from the fall of Rome to the rise of new powers. The Franks conquer Italy, the popes gain temporal rule, and Charlemagne is crowned, restoring a Roman name in the West while Germanic states take shape. Then the narrative turns east, to Arabia and its peoples.

There Gibbon tells of Mahomet, his preaching at Mecca, his flight to Medina, and the spread of Islam, which would reshape three continents. Milman's notes guide the reader. The volume joins West and East in one sweep, and it is essential for following Rome's legacy into the Middle Ages.
975-ethics-part-5:
Baruch Spinoza's Ethics closes in Part Five, of the power of the understanding, or of human freedom, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Spinoza now passes to the way leading to freedom, treating the power of the mind over the emotions and the love of God that follows from true knowledge.

He argues that freedom is not free will, but understanding necessity, and that the mind that knows God finds blessedness in that knowledge. His geometric proofs reach their summit here, austere and hopeful at once. Part Five completes Spinoza's system, and it rewards readers who have followed him from God to freedom.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 5 of Mark Twain's A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court stages the restoration of the fountain. Merlin sweats over smoke-powders and spells for days while Hank's men quietly repair the broken pipe underground, then fireworks announce the water's return to a crowd of pilgrims. Merlin, beaten at his own trade, is put to sleep by a new magic — a wire, a battery, and a Yankee who understands both.

Afterward Hank holds a competitive examination for army commissions, judging officers on knowledge instead of birth, and starts the kingdom's first newspaper. Each triumph teaches the same lesson in a new field: trained skill beats inherited rank. Yet the Church and the old order watch his reforms closely, and a reader can feel the reckoning being stored up.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-5:
William Dean Howells opens the fifth and final part with the affairs of Every Other Week settled, on the surface, into their wonted form. Basil March, though, feels impermanency in everything, and shame toward Lindau, the old socialist his candor failed. He never told Lindau plainly whose money paid them both.

The closing volume gathers the novel's reckonings: a streetcar strike, the Dryfoos family broken by grief, and the Marches weighing their own comfort against their conscience. Howells ends without trumpets, in talk and quiet decisions. The full novel stands as his deepest study of American money, labor, and the literary life built on top of both.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Volume five of Breasted's Ancient Records of Egypt, published in 1906, is the indices volume for the whole corpus. It holds no new narrative inscriptions; its work is to unlock the four volumes before it. Breasted indexes kings, gods, places, titles, and Egyptian words across thousands of translated records.

A scholar tracing one pharaoh or one temple town can find every mention in the set from these pages. Such apparatus decides whether a corpus serves daily research or sits admired and unused. Breasted, a exacting organizer, understood that and built the indices with care. The volume completes the foundational English corpus of Egyptian historical texts. Libraries still keep the five volumes within arm's reach of the reading desks.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-5:
Hippolytus and Cyprian anchor volume five of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, in the Roberts and Donaldson edition of 1885. Both were third-century churchmen who quarreled with bishops of Rome. Caius and Novatian, smaller figures of the same stormy age, fill out the volume with an appendix.

Hippolytus gives the Refutation of All Heresies, a guided tour of every error he could name. Cyprian of Carthage writes on the unity of the church and the lapsed who fled persecution. His letters show a bishop holding his flock together under Decius's terror. The volume is the early church at its most argumentative and brave.
arabian-nights-payne-1883-vol-5:
In 1883 Payne's fifth volume of the Thousand Nights and One Night joined the growing shelf. The tales from the Calcutta edition grow ever more tangled and strange, as Shahrazad's store seems bottomless. John Payne's complete English version, the first of its kind, holds its course without expurgation.

Halfway through the set, the reader has crossed seas of story: islands of magnets, brass cities, and fish that speak. Each tale resets the pattern of wonder, danger, and narrow escape. Volume V stands at the center of Payne's nine, proof of his patience as a translator of the vast Arabic cycle.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-5:
Volume five of Michael L. Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud holds Tract Pesachim, the laws of Passover. Rodkinson's set, in its 1918 edition, was the first complete English Talmud. Passover is the great feast of the Exodus, and its rules fill daily life for weeks before it comes.

The rabbis work through the search for leaven, the burning of what is found, and the slaughter of the Passover lamb. Then comes the seder itself: the four cups, the telling of the story, and the order of the meal. Hard cases crowd in, from dough left rising to a lamb roasted whole. The volume is the Talmud's fullest picture of a festival kept at home and in the Temple.
bancroft-history-us-vol-5:
Independence is declared and defended in the fifth volume of Bancroft's History, from 1856. The early campaigns of the Revolutionary War unfold in harsh detail. George Washington emerges as the central figure of the American story.

Bancroft's democratic epic reaches its heroic phase in these pages. Defeats teach the raw army its trade, while endurance wins the day. He honors the common soldier beside the great commander. The volume shows why his history shaped how Americans pictured their founding war. It was a people's struggle, blessed by purpose and led by a man of rare virtue.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-5:
The fifth volume of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career runs from chapter thirty-four to chapter forty-one. The face of Renée, Nevil's French wife, returns to trouble his English courtship. A ride in the wrong direction turns pursuit into farce and danger. Old Dr. Shrapnel, assaulted and defenceless, demands an apology from the Earl of Romfrey.

Cecilia Halkett is conquered, chapter by chapter, by Nevil's blunt devotion. Rosamund, the loyal housekeeper, carries messages and warnings between the camps. A trial of Nevil ends in a lame victory, honour satisfied at a limp. Meredith entangles the apology plot with the love plot until neither can move alone. These chapters show his gift for scenes where pride must kneel and cannot. The Romfrey temper remains the true antagonist.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-5:
Survival, not conquest, marks the fifth volume of Carlyle's Frederick the Great, in the 1897 printing. The Seven Years' War grinds to its close at last. Frederick, battered but unbowed, also takes his share in the partition of Poland.

Odds that should have crushed Prussia fail to finish it. Carlyle honors sheer staying power as the highest proof of greatness. The hero ages before our eyes, victorious yet alone. His epic of endurance draws toward its end here. The king's fame stands secured, and his kingdom is hardened by seven years of fire and want. He never pretends the cost was small or the glory clean.

cinq-mars-volume-5:
Alfred de Vigny stages the reckoning of conspiracy in Cinq-Mars, Volume 5 of the English edition. De Thou, the hero's friend, confronts Cinq-Mars in a room. His charge is plain: the plot now means banishing or slaying a minister, and bringing a foreign army into France. Assassin and traitor are the words he forces his friend to hear.

The treaty with Spain, France's enemy, has carried the favorite far past pride into treason. Cinq-Mars leans at the chimneypiece, while his friend crosses his arms and judges him. Love for Marie de Gonzague, ambition, and hatred of Richelieu all get weighed in the scene. De Vigny slows the action to let conscience speak at full length. Readers near the end watch friendship do what armies could not: strip the plot of its romance. The scaffold casts its shadow, though the arrests and trial wait in the last volume.
curtius-history-greece-vol-5:
Fallen cities and rising Macedon fill the fifth volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1899 version. Philip builds an army and a kingdom in the north. Alexander then carries Greek arms to the ends of the known world.

Freedom fades as the city-states pass under kings, yet Greek culture conquers its conquerors. The Hellenistic world spreads language, art, and learning far and wide. Curtius closes his great work on that rich paradox. Readers leave with a full arc, from tribal legend to world empire, told by a scholar who loved Greece in its glory and its fall alike.
diana-of-the-crossways-volume-5:
The fifth and final volume of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways covers chapters thirty-six to forty-three. Champions of the stricken lady gather at Diana's door each morning. Sullivan Smith and Arthur Rhodes keep their punctilious rival watch. Diana, accused and ill, passes through convalescence of a distraught mind.

Nature receives one of her cultivated daughters in a short country excursion. The penultimate chapter shows a final struggle for liberty, run into harness at last. A nuptial chapter closes the book, as a barely willing woman is led to bloom with married feeling. Meredith rewards Diana's long defence of her honour with the steady Redworth. The volume completes a novel about talk, scandal, and a woman's claim to judge her own life.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-5:

The second triumvirate posts its death lists and crushes the tyrannicides at Philippi. Octavian then wars on Sextus Pompeius at sea and turns west against Antony. Dio keeps the senate debates and street feel of the crisis. These books carry the story to the last clash at Actium, told in the next volume.

ethics-part-5:
Benedict de Spinoza finishes his Ethics, in Elwes's translation, with part five, Of the Power of the Understanding, or of Human Freedom. His preface promises to show how far reason can control the emotions and what mental freedom, or blessedness, really is. The wise man, he says, proves far more powerful than the ignorant.

Spinoza argues that understanding an emotion clearly already loosens its grip, and that the mind's intellectual love of God is eternal. Things distinctly understood, the scholia insist, outweigh confused impressions in shaping a life. The Ethics ends on its highest claim: blessedness is not virtue's reward but virtue itself. These closing propositions complete the geometric system begun with definitions of God.
evan-harrington-volume-5:

India arrives in Following the Equator, Part 5, by Mark Twain, and boyhood dreams of the East take over. Twain writes that the old visions rise in a luscious moonlight: barbaric gorgeousness, princely titles, and names that taste good in the mouth. He lists them with delight, from the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Maharajah of Travancore to the Begum of Bhopal and the Gaikwar of Baroda.

Chapter XXXIX opens with a calendar maxim about learning to endure another man's adversity, which suits the imperial tour ahead. Even the great god Vishnu, Twain jokes, carries one hundred eight holy names for Sunday use, of which he once memorized all and now retains only John W. The Indian chapters that follow mix pageantry with hard reporting on famine, plague, and caste, but the doorway is this wonder: a famous humorist admitting the East still dazzles him.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-5:

The volume reflects on his life's work like a summing up for a jury. He weighs loss and gain across eight centuries of consequence. English freedom, he argues, survived by absorbing its conquerors. Readers get the reflective close of a vast history. The year 1066 stands as the hinge on which England's later story turns. Scholars still test their own views against his bold claims today.
froude-history-england-vol-5:

Plots at home and pressure abroad test her nerve from the start. The volume launches the reign that dominates the rest of his history, and it shows a queen determined, above all, to survive and to rule.

Even in fragments, the agenda-setting shows through. Molotov reads out items: the German fleet's division, reparations, and the Polish question. Trusteeships and the Italian colonies come up, as does Franco's Spain. Stalin insists Yalta did not decide Poland's frontiers. On Spain, he argues the Franco regime was imposed by Germany and Italy and shelters fascist remnants. Light touches survive too, in talk of meeting hours and late rising habits. The notes are prized precisely because they are raw, taken down as the words were spoken.

Edward Gibbon's fifth volume, with Milman's notes, opens at chapter forty-nine with the worship and persecution of images in the east. The fifth volume of Humboldt's Cosmos, in Otté's English translation, is the last, left unfinished at his death in 1859. The Bohn set had begun in 1849. Humboldt, near ninety, was still adding to it, on the geology of the earth and the distribution of life.

The volume returns to volcanoes and the making of rock, then closes on the geography of plants, the seed Humboldt planted with his Andean plant zones. Even unfinished, it completes the arc: from nebulae to the moss on a single mountainside. Cosmos as a whole was the Victorian age's grandest picture of one connected nature. Its author died the same year as Darwin's Origin appeared.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
The fifth volume of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Williams's translation, came out in 1821. The expedition is now in the Andes of New Granada and Quito. Humboldt climbs the great volcanoes, measuring their height against the sea and snow line.

On Chimborazo in 1802 he reached higher than any European had climbed, until thin air and a ravine stopped him short of the top. The volume's pages on altitude, plant zones stacked by height, and ancient Inca roads made seedbeds for whole sciences. Humboldt also copies and ponders the ruins and calendars of the peoples before the conquest. The Narrative's seventh volume would end the set in 1829.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-5:
Julian the Apostate, the emperor who tried to restore pagan worship, strides through Ibsen's vast double drama Emperor and Galilean. The fifth volume of Archer's 1908 edition presents both parts. Ibsen called the sprawling work his masterpiece, above even the famous social plays.

Two worlds collide in Julian: the beauty-loving pagan past and the Galilean faith he renounced. Philosophy, politics, and mysticism crowd the stage across decades of one reign. Rarely performed whole, the play reads like an epic of the spirit in crisis. It marks Ibsen's most ambitious reach as a thinker. Readers who know only the drawing-room dramas will find a different, grander Ibsen here.
ihne-history-rome-vol-5:
Caesar and civil war close Ihne's History of Rome in this fifth volume, from 1871. The republic's last giants fight for mastery of the Roman world. From their wars the Empire is born, and the free state passes into one-man rule.

Ihne ends his five books at the hinge of Western history. His German thoroughness carries the tale from Marius's heirs to Augustus's dawn. Readers see both the glory and the cost of the change. The full history served as a standard account for a generation, and its final volume shows the sober craft that earned that standing in full.
isbe-1915-vol-5:

By the final volume, thousands of signed articles by scholars covered the whole field of biblical study.

The closing volume carries the alphabet to its end and adds maps, lists, and indexes that tie the set together. Readers could trace a name, a place, or a doctrine across all five volumes. The encyclopedia became the standard companion to Bible study for pastors and students of its era. Though later works replaced it, its articles still reward readers who want the learning of 1915 in one place.
jataka-cowell-vol-5:
The fifth volume of Cowell's Jataka, published in 1905, nears the end of the 547 birth stories. E. B. Cowell edited the set at Cambridge, and several hands translated from the Pali. Only one volume remained after this one in the 1895 to 1907 series.

The tales here are among the longest in the collection, full of travel, war, and royal intrigue. The future Buddha, born as prince or sage, holds to truth and mercy when courts reward neither. Each story still ends with the Buddha naming the cast in their present lives. The volume carries the cycle's growing weight toward its famous finale.
joshua-volume-5:
Volume five of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens at chapter twenty-four, on a prisoner transport bound for the mines. The captain of the guards has never had a harder trip. One prisoner, Ephraim, has escaped, and his faithful hounds are lost. Two storms have drenched and terrified the troop, the second fiercer than any in twenty-five years of service.

Fever struck prisoners and guards alike after their wet nights in the open. Two dead prisoners had to be buried on the road. Hosea, linked to the bold lad who fled, suffers most from the captain's ill humor. Yet he bears every hardship in silence, without complaint or oaths. This volume follows the Hebrews' suffering as Pharaoh's army meets its end.
journeys-through-bookland-vol-5:
Volume five of Journeys Through Bookland, in the 1922 new edition, turns toward heroes and legends for young readers. Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels opens the contents. King Arthur follows, with Balin and Balan, the Holy Grail from Malory, and Arthur's passing. Tennyson supplies Geraint and Enid and The Passing of Arthur in verse.

Shakespeare enters through Polonius's advice, and Cardinal Newman's Lead, Kindly Light as a hymn. James Whitcomb Riley and Michael Drayton add lighter and patriotic verse. Later pieces tell of Henry Hudson's fourth voyage and Robert Bruce and the spider. Sylvester steers older children from story toward history and national legend in this volume.
lawyer-quince-odd-craft-part-5:
W. W. Jacobs wrote Lawyer Quince as part of his story collection Odd Craft. Quince is a bootmaker in the village of Little Haven. His neighbors gave him his nickname for a clear reason.

From a few old law books, Quince gained much legal lore. He offers that lore freely to anyone with a dispute. Jacobs opens on a sunny, sleepy village street after the London coach. Footsteps and raised voices then promise a fresh quarrel. Jacobs tells such village tales with dry, affectionate humor. Jacobs sets the tale among his Little Haven villagers. Quince's book learning meets village cunning with comic results.
lecky-england-18th-vol-5:
Revolution shocks England in the fifth volume of Lecky's History, from 1890. France's upheaval kindles reform hopes at home and loyalist fears beside them. The younger Pitt fights to hold the nation together through a decade of passion and panic.

Radicals and loyalists battle for the country's soul in Lecky's pages. Trials for treason, cheap pamphlets, and volunteer corps mark the divide. He maps the passions of the seventeen nineties with wide learning and calm judgment. The volume shows Britain's great political split at its sharpest, a crisis that set the terms of debate for the century to come.
life-of-george-washington-volume-1-of-5:
Washington Irving opens his five-volume life of Washington here. Chapter One traces the Washington family's ancient English genealogy. The family held landed estates in the county of Durham. Its roots reach back to the century after the Norman Conquest.

William the Conqueror rewarded followers after wasting the northern country. The shrine of St. Cuthbert made Durham a rich, privileged see. Camden's Britannia supplies Irving's early authorities and color. From these deep roots, Irving builds toward Washington's Virginia youth. St. Cuthbert's shrine drew princes and gentry as a titular defence. William increased Durham's extraordinary privileges after the Conquest.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-5:
Part Five opens with Twain receiving his pilot's license. Chapter 21 calls itself a section in his biography. Steady work followed, and he hoped to die at the wheel. Then the war came and suspended river commerce entirely.

Twain became a Nevada silver miner, then a newspaper reporter. Gold mining, San Francisco reporting, and Sandwich Islands correspondence followed. Twenty-one years drifted before he saw the pilot-house again. Chapter 22 then returns him to the river he loved. Lecture platforms and New England authorship ended his wandering list. A poet companion joined the return trip down the river.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-5:
Volume 5 closes George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta with Book 5. It opens with 'Lovers Mated,' as Lord Ormont thinks of Aminta as his countess. Yet the old soldier still broods on how wives should be ruled, in Napoleon's way.

Farewell visits and a marine duet lead toward the plighting, the lovers' pledge. A chapter gives Aminta's own words to her lord before the conclusion. Meredith ends the long contest of pride and patience on the coast. The volume settles whether love or pride rules this marriage. It completes one of Meredith's most searching stories of married life.
marion-arleigh-s-penance-everyday-life-l:
Marion Arleigh's Penance was number five in Chicago's Everyday Life Library. Charlotte M. Brame, also spelled Braeme here, wrote it. She was the author of Dora Thorne and other beloved tales. The story opens at three o'clock on a warm June afternoon in London.

Heat lies on the city like a purple haze over a sapphire sky. No breath of wind stirs the leaves or cools the workers. Against that sultry opening, Marion's story of love and penance unfolds. Brame wrote for the great public that devoured weekly fiction. Her tales joined high romance to humble life. Penance, in her world, is the price of a proud heart's lesson.
matrimonial-openings-sailor-s-knots-part:
W. W. Jacobs placed Matrimonial Openings in his Sailor's Knots set of 1909. Mr. Dowson sits by the kitchen fire and smokes in peace. His wife talks hot and fast while he gives mild answers.

She fears their daughter Flora will wed as her sister Jenny did. Jenny's match, she says, left her worn with work. Flora walks out with Charlie Foss, a man her mother calls good for nothing. Ben Lippet, who will one day be his own master, is her mother's pick. Jacobs lets the wife's sharp talk clash with the man's calm replies. The humor rests on that clash more than on the courtship itself.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book five of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at the waters of Bourbonne. Few guests had come that year when the tale starts. The Prince de Mont-Beliard of Wurtemberg soon arrives to pay his respects.

He had lost his wife less than a year before that visit. French officers held his states, and he feared the hold would last. He dared not ask her plainly what the King meant to do. Chancellor Hyde, who had swapped houses with her, brings word of his wish. A note from the King and a letter from her husband follow. Land in Navarre, promised to her, hangs in the air.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-5:
Government, not emperors, fills the fifth volume of Merivale's History, from 1863. Merivale pauses his tale of courts and camps to show the working Empire. Tax men, roads, courts, and provincial towns reveal how Rome was actually run from day to day.

Daily business replaces drama in these instructive pages. Grain fleets, post roads, and local councils keep a world in motion. He shows the slow rhythms that held millions in one system. The volume gives readers the Empire's machinery in full view. Most histories of Rome stop at the palace door, so the turn is rare and valuable.
nasa-tm-19640008185-satellite-situation-: Volume four, number five of NASA's satellite situation report series is preserved here. Reports in the series were compiled by Goddard Space Flight Center with NORAD and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. They catalog satellites and other objects in orbit, with launch and orbital data. The hosted sample preserves only garbled table data with no readable text, so this issue's date and listings cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19710010490-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Panel 5A of the Apollo 13 Investigation Team owned corrective action for the Command and Service Modules. Its study, dated June 12, 1970, began right after the flight that lost its number two oxygen tank. Panel leader A. C. Cahen approved the report, which covers both studying fixes and putting them into effect.

The contents map three jobs. First comes the cryogenic oxygen tank failure, then an accidental fuel cell reactant valve closure. A third section compares configuration differences among service modules 108, 109, and 110. Appendices cover oxygen quantity gaging, stratification, heater analysis, and service procedures prepared for Apollo 14. The scope section says the panel also assessed possible problems flagged by a related systems evaluation panel. Together the sections form the corrective action record for the next CSM flights.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-5:
Augustine's anti-Pelagian writings fill volume five of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, from 1886. Philip Schaff edited the set. Pelagius, a British monk, had taught that humans can choose the good by their own strength. Augustine spent his last twenty years fighting that teaching.

The treatises here argue that grace is not a reward for merit but the source of every good act. Original sin, infant baptism, and predestination all come under his hammer. The fight fixed the West's doctrine of grace for good and ill. Augustine's late severity still sparks argument; few sets of pages have shaped more sermons.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-5:
Gregory of Nyssa, youngest of the three great Cappadocians, fills volume five of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, with his dogmatic treatises and other works. Gregory was Basil's brother and the deepest thinker of the three. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace edited the series.

His Great Catechism teaches the faith's whole frame to new instructors. Against Eunomius he defends the Trinity with careful logic about names and knowledge. His life of his sister Macrina, and his talks on the soul and resurrection held as she lay dying, give the volume a human close. Gregory's teaching on the soul's endless growth toward God still draws readers.
night-and-morning-volume-5:
Book the Fifth, the last book of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning, fills volume five. A Latin line from Petronius heads chapter one, about the mysteries and ministerings of the gods. A note in the copy points readers to a corrected full set in Project Gutenberg.

Mr Roger Morton stands behind his counter on a drizzling, melancholy day. Morton is an alderman, twice mayor of his native town, and a thriving man grown portly. Nightly brandy and water have deepened the roses on his cheek. His digestion troubles him, and he blames joint, pudding, vegetables, and cigars in turn. The brandy he never thinks of dropping.
northern-lights-volume-5:
Volume five closes Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights with three tales: The Error of the Day, The Whisperer, and As Deep as the Sea. The first opens with a definition from an Admiralty note. The error of the day is the gap between the range set on a gun's sights and the true range.

A great naval gun, Parker notes, never fires twice alike. Air, ammunition, and wear shift its aim, so allowance must be made each time. Talk then turns to Kowatin, in the Saskatchewan country. Billy Goat, really William Goatry, sings a street song about a fatherless child. Parker mixes sea gunnery and prairie talk in one volume.
one-of-our-conquerors-volume-5:
George Meredith closed his novel in this fifth volume. Book five opens with Nesta and her father. Victor rides with Lady Grace Halley in her carriage. She flatters him that together they might rule the world. The thought exposes the poor value of his aim.

Mother and daughter meet in the next chapter. Nataly, Nesta, and Dartrey Fenellan share a key scene. A chapter stands in the shadow of Mrs. Marsett. An expiation and a great undelivered speech follow. The last chapter ends Victor's campaign of ambition. Meredith ends with irony, pity, and hard self-knowledge.
pahlavi-texts-west-vol-5:
West closed his five-volume Pahlavi Texts with a final volume in 1897. It appeared as volume forty-seven of the Sacred Books of the East. The volume translates books eight and nine of the Dinkard.

The Dinkard, meaning Acts of Religion, is Zoroastrianism's great encyclopedia. Book eight summarizes lost Avestan texts book by book in detail. Book nine expounds selected passages with commentary and moral teaching. West's rendering closed his long labor of preservation in 1897. Together the five volumes gave English readers a Zoroastrian library. The series stands as the last word of a monumental Victorian project. Later scholars still build on West's foundations.
palfrey-history-new-england-vol-5:
Palfrey closes his great History of New England with Volume 5, from 1858. The story runs through the eighteenth century to the eve of revolt. Five volumes end as the Puritan world gives way to an American one.

New wealth, new ideas, and new wars loosen the old tight bonds. Town faith yields ground to trade, print, and wider horizons each year. Palfrey keeps his calm, full style to the final chapter. His work stood for decades as the standard history of the region. The close feels earned: a world ends, and another waits offstage.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
Volume five of Frazer's Pausanias gathers the maps and plans of the edition. Frazer's 1898 Description of Greece used text, commentary, and now cartography. Readers can walk the traveler's routes with these sheets in hand.

Plans of sanctuaries and cities show walls, temples, and excavated remains. Topographical essays argue how routes ran between ancient sites. The visual companion turns armchair reading into a field expedition. Frazer believed ancient texts should be tested against the ground itself. His maps embodied that belief for a generation of travelers. Archaeologists carried these volumes to Greece in their luggage for decades. The volume completes the working apparatus of the great commentary.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Part 5 of volume 2 of Sheridan's memoirs, the contents pages, with no chapter text visible. The contents run from the battle of Dinwiddie Court House and Five Forks through Sailor's Creek to the meeting of Grant and Lee and the surrender. Later chapters take Sheridan to Texas, the Rio Grande, and the French invasion of Mexico, then to Reconstruction duty in Louisiana and Texas.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-5:
Part 5 of Grant's memoirs opens at chapter fifty-two, the battle of Spotsylvania in May 1864. Grant explains the ground with an engineer's care: the Mattapony River and its four little parent streams, the Mat, the Ta, the Po, and the Ny. Lee's army comes up by the Catharpin Road while Warren and Hancock take the Brock Road.

Burnside crosses the Ny and holds against a furious attack. Grant reads Lee's movements and prepares to strike his right and get between him and Richmond. The part is the Overland Campaign at closest quarters, generalship written as plain narrative.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
The fifth and last volume of Gilbert Parker's Pierre and His People contains Antoine and Angelique, The Cipher, A Tragedy of Nobodies, and A Sanctuary of the Plains. These closing tales stay in the far north world of the earlier volumes, where winter, distance, and small settlements press hard on the people in them.

Antoine and Angelique opens as quiet dialogue between husband and wife watching birds go south early, a sign the winter will be long. Angelique has heard a child cry in the night and felt a cold hand at her heart; Antoine answers each fear gently, blaming devil-birds and wild geese. The exchange builds a mood of dread before she asks that they, too, go southward before the great winds come.
plato-dialogues-jowett-vol-5:
The fifth and last volume of Plato in Benjamin Jowett's translation is given wholly to the Laws. The Laws is Plato's longest work and the last he wrote. Gone is Socrates; an unnamed Athenian stranger talks with two old men on a walk through Crete.

The three design a new colony, Magnesia, law by law: its gods, its schools, its marriages, its courts, and its drinking parties. The tone is stricter and more pious than the Republic's, with heavy stress on law as teacher. Some editions add Plato's letters to the volume's plan. Reading the Laws shows Plato in old age, trading the ideal city for one men might actually build.
ranke-history-england-vol-5:
Volume 5 of Ranke's History, from 1875, brings the Stuarts to the throne. James I rules first, with his claims of divine right held high. The long road toward civil war opens across these careful pages.

Ranke traces the deep clash between king and parliament step by step. Money, faith, and law feed a crisis neither side can calm. His long view, the hallmark of his work, holds the whole span. Small slights grow into fixed camps and armed camps in time. The storm gathers slowly, and the historian misses none of its signs. Readers watch a kingdom drift toward a breaking point it cannot see.
rhoda-fleming-volume-5: The fifth volume of Rhoda Fleming by George Meredith is preceded here only by the standard header of its plain-text publisher. It supplies the title, the author's name, and English as the language of the text, and it counts the item as the thirty-first in a series of Meredith's works. No memoir of the story follows it in the pages shown: neither a contents list nor an opening scene is printed. Only the facts of title, author, and volume five can be reported from this front matter.
roughing-it-part-5:
Part 5 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, in an 1880 printing, opens at Chapter XLI with Captain Nye sick with spasmodic rheumatism, a joint disease marked by sharp pains. Nye is kind and pleasant when at ease. When a spasm hits, he groans, wails, and swears with great force and fancy. The narrator bears it gladly, since he had seen Nye nurse a sick man with patience when the roles were reversed.

While Nye raves, the narrator's mind stays busy night and day with grand plans. He redraws his house, weighs a billiard-room in the attic, and picks between green and blue cloth for the drawing-room. He plans servants, a fine home for his mother, and a grand trip through Europe. He writes home each day with orders about land and money.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-5:
Part 5 of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren, written as Josiah Allen's Wife, opens at Chapter XVIII with Samantha reading her husband's face. Josiah's face was smooth and placid, and he had not taken a mite of sense of what she had been saying, and she knew it. Men, she reflects, know at most that it is only talk, since women have not got it in their power to do anything. His accent was mildly wondering and gently sarcastic. How a steeple would look pointing down, he said: that is a true woman's idea. A picture of Sister Filkins is printed in the passage.

Samantha answers that she would have the steeple point down toward the depths of darkness in the heart of the man who raised it up.
sandra-belloni-volume-5: Volume 5 of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni, marked v5, is presented here through header matter only, as number 23 in a series by the author. The title line names the work and the author, and a release date of September 2003 is given. The file was first posted on January 4, 2002, as Etext number 4417, in Edition 10, in English and ASCII. A credit line names Pat Castevans and David Widger as producers of the electronic text. Nothing from the novel's pages appears in the portion shown here.
satapatha-brahmana-eggeling-vol-5:
Eggeling's fifth and final Satapatha Brahmana volume appeared in 1900. It closed the Sacred Books of the East rendering of the great Vedic ritual manual. Eggeling had spent nearly two decades on the translation project.

The closing books contain a famous jewel, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. There, talk of ritual turns into deep thought about the self. Teachers like Yajnavalkya debate the nature of the soul and ultimate reality. Sacrifice gives way to philosophy across these chapters. The volume thus marks the hinge between old Vedic worship and Indian thought. Eggeling's completion of the set was a major scholarly achievement.
sketches-new-and-old-part-5:
Mark Twain's sketches new and old continue in this fifth part, opening with The Siamese Twins, written about 1868. Twain claims close knowledge of the joined brothers and promises private details never before in print. The twins, he reports, stayed fast bound to each other through decades of travel and fame.

Even as children they played together always, so that their mother hunted for one when both were lost, sure the other stood near. Twain turns their bond into a rebuke of civilized brothers who quarrel and part. Tenderness and satire share the sketch in equal measure.
stepping-backwards-night-watches-part-5:
Stepping Backwards belongs to Night Watches, a set of comic tales by W. W. Jacobs about working men talking in pubs. Mr. Simpson has just had new teeth fitted at dinner-time, and his friend Mr. Jack Mills praises the change, saying the lisp is gone and the teeth make him look far younger than his fifty-three years.

Mills then pushes a fuller make-over: shave the whiskers, dye the white hair black, and do it all at once at a barber's shop in Bird Street. Simpson hesitates, half tempted and half afraid of being laughed at, and the humor grows from vanity, friendship, and the wish to seem young again at the warehouse.
stories-by-american-authors-volume-5:
Stories by American Authors, Volume V, dated 1884, holds A Light Man by Henry James, Yatil by F. D. Millet, The End of New York by Park Benjamin, Why Thomas Was Discharged by George Arnold, and The Tachypomp by E. P. Mitchell.

James opens the volume with a diary-like tale. A man home again after years away feels bored and low. He resumes his old notes in April 1857. He weighs what he seems to friends, to a woman he may love, and to himself. Around it sit tales of war, work, and a famed speed machine, giving a mixed shelf of serious and fanciful American writing.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-5:
Volume 5 of Symonds's Renaissance in Italy, from 1875, treats the Catholic reaction. The free world of the early age meets a sterner church. Discipline returns, and the spring of Italy fades toward dusk.

Councils, censors, and new orders press on thought and art alike. Symonds closes the age proper with Rome's firm reassertion of rule. Painters and thinkers learn to work within tight, watched bounds here. He mourns the lost freedom while granting the new order its strength. Freedom yields to order in his sad, balanced telling of events. The sunset he paints has shadow, gold, and grief in it.
talleyrand-memoirs-vol-5:
The fifth and final volume of Talleyrand's memoirs brings his long career to its close. After the July Revolution of 1830, the aged diplomat took one last post: ambassador to London. Beaufort's translation completes the 1891 set.

Talleyrand recalls the July Monarchy and his London mission, where he worked to keep peace between France and Britain. Belgium's future and Europe's balance fill these final chapters. He writes as a man summing up a life spent in every regime. Few memoirs span so many governments with one cool, constant voice. He died in 1838, soon after the London years this volume recalls.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: No prose by Meredith stands here for volume five. The book is The Adventures of Harry Richmond. A Gutenberg wrapper stands in its stead. The part is numbered 54 in its set. It is filed as 4448. Release is dated September 2003. First posting was January 31, 2002. David Widger is named as the file's maker.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-5:
Part five of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter eighteen by giving away Tom's great secret. He and his brother pirates schemed to come home and attend their own funerals.

The boys had paddled on a log to the Missouri shore at dusk on Saturday and slept in the woods at the town's edge. They then crept through back lanes and dozed in the church gallery amid broken benches. At Monday breakfast Aunt Polly and Mary shower Tom with love and care. Polly grants the joke was fine, yet calls him hard-hearted for letting her suffer near a week. Readers get the funeral scene and Tom's brief glow of fame.
the-amazing-marriage-volume-5:
Book Five closes George Meredith's 1895 novel in this fifth volume. Its chapters run from The Red Warning from a Son of Vapour onward. A last chapter ends with a parting word by the Dame. Along the way come a retarded courtship, a road to an act of penance, and a meeting of earl, countess, and her brother over a silver cross.

The opening finds Fleetwood at his leased estate of Calesford, worn down by tradesmen rushing to make the house fit for grand London parties. At dinner Gower Woodseer, acting as secretary, forces him to hear how bad Countess Livia's money troubles have grown, with gambling debts bleeding her dry.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Volume five of Gilbert Parker's romance opens at chapter thirty-one on a dark night at St Aubin's Bay. Ranulph returns home to find no light, no drawn blinds, and no fire. He fears something has happened to his father before he reaches the door.

Dormy Jamais hurries round the corner, plucks his sleeve, and refuses to talk indoors because stone walls have ears. Dormy says he has Ranulph's father safe and chuckles at his own cleverness. Speaking in Jersey patois, Ranulph humours the shrewd little man. Dormy then runs toward the shore, his wooden shoes clacking, whispering that there has been trouble in St Heliers.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-5:
October 1885, volume three, number five, opens with a portrait of William W. Crapo and a sketch by Edward P. Guild. Crapo of New Bedford is presented through his father first. Henry Howland Crapo, son of a Dartmouth farmer, taught himself with so little help that he once set out to make his own dictionary.

Henry became a teacher, surveyor, city treasurer, and library trustee, with interests in the whale fisheries. After timber purchases in Michigan he moved there, entered politics, and served four years as governor from 1865. William, born in Dartmouth on May 16, 1830, was his only son among ten children and shared his love of learning.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum: Volume 5 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters XXIX to XLI, printed at Dublin in 1839. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapters promise Captain Trevanion's adventure, difficulties, an explanation, Mr. O'Leary's first and second loves, a duel, and early recollections of a first love. Later titles turn to wise resolves, the proposal, and thoughts on matrimony in general and in the army in particular. No chapter text follows.
the-convert-deep-waters-part-5:
W. W. Jacobs tells The Convert as part of his Deep Waters stories. Mr. Purnip walks arm in arm with Mr. Billing, a new recruit to his cause, and praises him warmly. With Billing won over, Purnip says, the others will follow like sheep, and his friend will shine as a bright lamp in the darkness.

Billing is pleased but unsure of the rules. He has given up fighting, yet he asks what to do if somebody hits him. Turn the other cheek, Purnip answers, and smile; shame will hurt the striker more than a blow. Billing doubts it, noting he can hit a man pretty hard and that a good smack in the jaw saves a deal of arguing. Purnip paints the sway a first-class fighting man gains by refusing to fight.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p:
Part five of Purgatory in Dante's Vision holds cantos twenty-six through thirty-three, in Cary's verse. Walking single file along a rim of flame, Dante casts a shadow that makes the fire burn redder. Spirits marvel that he seems no mere shade, and one begs to know how a living man can block the sun.

Poets of love pass through the fire and greet each other with joy. Past the flames, an angel sends Dante on to the earthly paradise. There he meets a lost love, confesses his faults, and is made clean for the stars.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-5:
An essay on Isaiah opens volume five of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations. It calls Isaiah the first and most sublime of the four greater Hebrew prophets, son of Amoz, who spoke under four kings of Judah. It also notes that many critics give the last twenty-seven chapters to a later writer, since Cyrus is named there.

Next comes the ruin of Sennacherib's host, when an angel slew a vast Assyrian camp in one night. Text and plate pairs fill the volume. Doré's portrait of the prophet is judged here to fit the later voice better.
the-elson-readers-book-5: The Elson Readers, Book Five, by William H. Elson and Christine M. Keck, is present here as title matter and a contents list. A tale called The Crystal Glass opens the book. Then comes a part named Nature, Humour, Home and Country. Animal pieces name Samuel White Baker, Ernest Harold Baynes, and Theodore Roosevelt. Bird and flower poems follow. No lesson text appears in these pages.
the-gilded-age-part-5:
Part 5 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter XXXVII. Laura Hawkins looks for a committee chairman. He is nowhere to be found. She makes a new plan. She sends a note to the Hon. Mr. Buckstone. She asks him to call that night.

Buckstone comes, and the two trade smooth praise. Laura plays on his fame as a man not fond of women. He replies with fine words about her own fame. Each one flatters the other. Each one seems pleased. The talk shows how charm works as a tool in Washington. A bill there can turn on a smile and a well-placed call.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-5:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 5 of that work. It opens with Chapter XVIII, Freedom Proclaimed to All. Logan takes up the question of emancipation as it came to a head. Much of Lincoln's thought, he says, turned on one perplexity. Lincoln assumed that the physical difference between the black and white races barred their living together in one land as free men and equals.

Logan traces that idea through Lincoln's speeches and acts. It was advanced in the Lincoln-Douglas debates. As President, Lincoln held out a hope to the border-state delegations on July 12, 1862. The freed people, he suggested, might go to his projected colony in South America. On August 14 he appealed to the colored free men on the same plan. The chapter shows emancipation weighed against colonization in Lincoln's mind.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Vol. 2, No. 5 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated February 3, 1898. It is also numbered No. 65 of the whole run. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a publisher's notice of rates. The paper comes from 3 and 5 West 18th Street, New York, every Thursday. Single numbers cost five cents each. The trade is supplied by the American News Company.
the-history-of-rome-volumes-1-5: Theodor Mommsen wrote The History of Rome. The record holds a compilation of the five volumes. William Purdie Dickson translated the work with the author's sanction. A note lists the five books in order. Book I covers the period before the end of the monarchy. Book V ends with the establishment of the military monarchy. The note adds that each volume stands on its own as well. Only the compilation note and title page are present here. A dedications heading also appears.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m: Volume 5 of The Mayflower and Her Log, by Azel Ames, is represented here only by its Project Gutenberg front wrapper. the-money-master-volume-5:
Volume 5 of Gilbert Parker's The Money Master contains Epoch the Fifth, chapters XXII to XXV, and an epilogue. the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-5:
Part 5 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XV, Tom as King. Foreign ambassadors come with gorgeous trains, and Tom, throned in awful state, receives them. The splendour delights him at first, but the long, dreary addresses wear the pleasure into homesickness. He says the words Hertford puts into his mouth and looks like a king, yet cannot feel like one. He is cordially glad when the ceremony ends.

Most of Tom's day is spent in labours of royal office. Even two hours of princely pastimes are fettered by ceremony. Only his private hour with his whipping-boy counts as clear gain, bringing both entertainment and needful information. By the third day he is growing used to his chains. One dread still looms over the fourth day: dining in public, alone, under a multitude of curious eyes.
the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-5:
Volume five of Gilbert Parker's The Seats of the Mighty holds chapters twenty-five to thirty of Captain Robert Moray's memoirs. Its headings include The Secret of the Tapestry and Master Devil Doltaire. An appendix excerpt from The Scot in New France follows the final chapter.

The twenty-fifth chapter, In the Cathedral, opens at dawn. Moray looks out over ruined Lower Town roofs at dawn. A bell calls to prayers at the Jesuit College. Starved peasants creep about the cathedral, eager for crumbs. Yet the Intendant's Palace holds abundance and revelry, Moray notes. He descends to the room where Labrouk's body lies. Candles burn at the dead man's head and feet. Labrouk's widowed wife enters, and Moray whispers his sympathy.
the-sisters-volume-5:
Volume five of Georg Ebers's The Sisters opens at chapter twenty-two, on a tower roof. An astrologer stood on the pylon tower by the gate of the Serapeum, Ebers writes. He had mounted to observe the stars. Swift black clouds kept sweeping across his field, though. At last he laid aside his instruments impatiently. No translator is named in the pages shown for this volume.

The gate-keeper, father of poor little Philo, answered with a shrug. It is a night of horror, he declared, and great disaster threatens. In fifteen years in his place he had seen such a night only once before. The next day Antiochus's soldiers plundered their treasury, he recalled. Tonight is worse, he insisted. The sacred bulls seemed to rise from the dead in the Apis-cave, butting at the door with their horns.

the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-volume-:
Volume five of Zola's Lourdes, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, covers the fifth day, and readers should note that no fourth-day volume sits among these records. Pierre again cannot sleep at the Hotel of the Apparitions. He has inquired after Marie, who sleeps soundly after the procession, and he worries that her father has not returned from Gavarnie. With the hare-brained M. de Guersaint, every mischance seems possible.

The last night of the pilgrimage fills the hotel with pilgrims hurrying to and from the Grotto, doors slamming and floors shaking. Pierre keeps rising, mistaking corridor noises for de Guersaint's return. Zola closes his Lourdes inquiry with a doubting priest kept awake by the very fervour he cannot share, while the cured and the unhealed prepare to leave.
the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volume-5:
Book Five of Zola's Paris, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens with Guillaume bent on witnessing the execution of Salvat, the anarchist. Pierre tries to dissuade him, fails, and resolves to spend the night at Montmartre watching over his brother. The guillotine can be seen from a Socialist deputy's house, so Pierre offers himself as guide. The brothers sit up in the workroom until two o'clock, then start out into a serene, moonlit night.

Paris below them sleeps like a spell-bound city, its labour and suffering lulled until dawn, while in a far district a knife is being raised to kill a man. The Sacred Heart basilica looms white and domeless over the roofs, a symbol of dominion. Zola sends his priest and his revolutionary to watch the state kill, testing both men's faiths at daybreak.
the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volume-5:
Part Five of Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens on the evening of Pierre's long-awaited papal audience, fixed for nine o'clock. He waits in the Borgo, early, his heart gripped by infinite emotion and grief. That afternoon he spent beside the dead Dario and Benedetta, who now lie in one another's arms. The lovers' pitiful end has left him unable to eat, longing only to hide and weep.

Walking slowly across the dark Piazza of St. Peter's, lit only by lamps around the obelisk and colonnade, he feels an anguish of charity for all who suffer. Zola brings his priest to the Pope carrying grief for Paris and Rome alike. Whether the audience heals or ends his dream of a rejuvenated Christianity is the trilogy's Roman question.

thirlwall-history-greece-vol-5:
Volume 5 of Thirlwall's History, from 1845, gives the Peloponnesian War itself. Athens and Sparta lock in a long, grinding death struggle here. Thirlwall follows Thucydides closely, and he follows him very well.

Plague, revolt, and the Sicilian disaster crush Athens by slow degrees. Sparta's patience and Persia's gold wear the sea empire down at last. The bishop's steady narrative never flinches from the war's waste. Greek disunity, not foreign arms, breaks the city-states in his telling. Readers feel the tragedy build year by grim campaigning year. His calm voice makes the horror land harder, not softer.
un-ga-res-a-69-5:
One state's trade laws can reach too far, argues Resolution A/69/5, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text defends a set of Charter-era rules: states are equal, none may meddle in the home affairs of others, and trade and shipping must run free. Heads of Ibero-American states had already called for an end to one-sided trade steps by one state against another.

The named target is the U.S. Helms-Burton Act of 12 March 1996, part of the U.S. embargo of Cuba. Its reach past U.S. borders, the text says, harms the rights of other states and of firms and people under their law. Year by year, this vote is the Assembly's standing rebuke of that law.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/5, adopted in the autumn of 2014, is the General Assembly's annual call to end the United States embargo against Cuba. The Assembly reaffirms sovereign equality, non-intervention, and freedom of trade and navigation. It expresses concern at laws with extraterritorial effects, such as the 1996 Helms-Burton Act. It again urges states that maintain such laws to repeal or invalidate them as soon as possible. It asks the Secretary-General to report on implementation at the seventieth session.
un-sc-res-5:
Soviet troops in Iran gave the young Security Council one of its first tests. Iran had reported that it could not yet confirm a full Soviet withdrawal. The statement came in a report dated 6 May 1946. Council rules set in April required that check. On 8 May 1946 the Council chose to wait rather than press on.

It deferred further proceedings on the Iranian matter. Iran needed time to verify the facts through its own officials. The government in Tehran had to report what it found. The Soviet Union was absent from the vote. The case showed the limits of the Council when a great power was itself a party.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Soviet troops remaining in Iran gave the newborn Council its first great test. Moscow had promised to withdraw by spring 1946. Iran reported on 6 May that it could not yet confirm a full pullout. Resolution 5 was adopted on 8 May 1946 by ten votes. The Soviet delegation was absent from the chamber.

Members chose to pause rather than escalate. Proceedings on the Iranian case were deferred. Tehran gained time to check through its own officials. A complete report was demanded as soon as possible. If Iran still lacked answers by 20 May, it had to report what it knew. The Council would then decide its next steps.

watch-dogs-ship-s-company-part-5:
W. W. Jacobs tells Watch-Dogs as one of his Ship's Company tales, in the voice of the oldest inhabitant of a waterside village. The tale opens at the Cauliflower inn. The old man takes a long, slow draught of beer, and calls it almost the only enjoyment he has left, that and a pipe of tobacco. Neither wants chewing, he notes. That is a great thing when a man has little left to chew with.

He lights his pipe with infinite care, cupping the match though the summer air is still. Then he lectures the wayfarer who bought his pint. Kindness to animals is all very well, he says, but kindness to your fellow creatures is more. A given pint earns thanks even once it is gone. When the landlord refills his mug unasked, the old man starts with pleasure and spills two spoonfuls.
